response.answer: To control multiplicity in exploratory analyses, use FDR for pre-specified families and define ROPE for practical significance. Hierarchical models may not require adjustments if pre-specified.

results.title: Understanding Multiplicity in Clinical Trials | Blog | Phastar
results.content: Recently, an FDA industry guidance draft on “Multiple Endpoints in Clinical Trials”1 provided an overview of multiplicity which is a controversial topic. This is due to the practitioner’s common lack of clarity on when and how it arises and what adjustments to implement, such that the number of false positives, i.e. the type I error rate is constrained to a pre-specified level of significance alpha when performing inference for multiple hypothesis tests simultaneously2. Some of the reasons which lead to multiplicity include: (1) multiple primary endpoints which are each individually relevant to address the primary study objective, (2) more than two treatment arms, i.e. multiple treatments, combinations of treatments or different doses of same treatment, (3) repeated measurements, i.e. an outcome measurement is recorded at different time points for each patient, (4) interim analysis and (5) subgroup analyses where patient outcomes may vary when sub-setting by variables, such as biomarker status, age group or diabetes status. The overall error rate of one or more type I errors is known as family-wise error rate (FWER) and is calculated as 1-(1-alpha)^k where k is the number of tests.

Title: Multiplicity in clinical trials with hierarchical strategy - interpret - Datamethods Discussion Forum
# Multiplicity in clinical trials with hierarchical strategy. In a clinical trial, when the study design includes a hierarchical analysis strategy, is the statistical adjustment for multiplicity no longer necessary? I want to be able to make conclusions (at the individual hypothesis level) of a secondary outcome (in the scenario in which the primary outcome was statistically significant). I read that in this cases is not necessary to do the statistical adjustment, but I want know the statistical basis that supports it. I hope that several others will respond to this important question. It’s good to step back for a moment and recognize the different camps:. If doing a frequentist analysis, the type of analysis must in need of a multiplicity adjustment is a “there exists” analysis, i.e., there exists an endpoint or a subgroup for which the treatment has benefit, where there is no pre-specification of the endpoint or subgroup. On the other hand, when you have strongly pre-specified a hierarchy and you are not doing a “there exists” analysis, Cook and Farewell state that keeping each hypothesis in context is adequate and no multiplicity adjustment is needed. Cook and Farewell’s approach involves maintaining context at all times. The order of reporting results for different endpoints is pre-specified, and all results are reported, even in journal article abstracts, in that order. That way the reader will be sure that you are not cherry-picking positive results. Unlike an \alpha-spending approach (that I never liked), you can make a statement about an endpoint whether or not previous endpoints in the hierarchy yielded positive evidence for efficacy. Cook and Farewell state this as being interested in marginal questions, e.g., we want to know whether a treatment reduced pain whether or not it reduces the risk of stroke. That being said I think it is often better to develop a unified hierarchical ordinal outcome for the primary efficacy analysis. ordering the research questions or 2. doing an alpha spending adjustment are acceptable, it might be worth considering the FDR procedure. results.title: Multiplicity in clinical trial: An ignored concept - Indian Journal of Dermatology, Venereology and Leprology
results.content: Multiplicity is an inevitable issue in the interpretation of clinical trial data. It is defined as the potential inflation of type-I error rate (or alpha level) related to simultaneous multiple testing of different outcomes or end-points of interest.,,,. Many studies with hypotheses related to secondary and exploratory objectives have used strategies to account for multiplicity.,,, The protocol in such studies states that no final inferences will be made from these exploratory tests. However, if prespecification of meaningful ordering is not feasible, then the end-points of interest are tested in what is known as a data-driven testing sequence, that is, from the most significant to the least or vice versa. For instance, *Bonferroni* test can be justified in clinical studies where the underlying principle is to test each hypothesis at the 0.05/n alpha level. In Step 2, end-point 2 is deemed significant if end-point 1 is significant in Step 1 and *P* ≤ 0.05 for end-point 2 or if end-point 1 nonsignificant followed by *P* ≤ 0.025 for end-point 2.

results.title: Multiple testing: when should we adjust for multiplicity? - StatsImprove
results.content: # Multiple testing: when should we adjust for multiplicity? In this post we will try to provide some tips on how a researcher could answer the fateful question: should I adjust or not the significance level for multiple testing? The problem of multiplicity is a problem that concerns almost all scientific research and has not got yet a complete and definitive answer. To make you understand the problem better, we will provide you an example of a paper published in 2014, that estimated the percentage of these jobs at around 50% in multi-arm trials. Although it is not possible to address the problem of multiplicity in depth, before leaving we try to understand briefly what we encounter when we ignore the presence of multiple testing in our study and do not adjust the level of a statistical significance.
